title: A standing migration failure mark has no operator door to clear it
body:
## Summary
migrate() refuses every open while a _migration_failures mark stands, and the only way to clear one is clearMigrationFailure(), which nothing outside packages/kernel/test calls.

## Description
packages/kernel/src/migrate.ts:27 says a failure mark is 'cleared by an operator act' and :210 exports clearMigrationFailure as 'the operator's act after fixing what failed'. `grep -rn clearMigrationFailure app lib pipeline workers` finds no caller: the app, the worker and every CLI open through openKernel, which closes the store and returns the refusal. The operator's only remedy is hand-written SQL against the live store. Fixed looks like a pipeline verb (e.g. `pipeline/kernel.mts migrations status|clear <module>`) that lists marks with their reason and the newest pre-migration snapshot, and clears one with a ledger event naming the operator.

## Flow
- a step fails once (or a deploy ships a bad step) -> mark written (migrate.ts:203)
- every later openKernel -> refused 'mark stands' (migrate.ts:83)
- the operator has no command to see or clear it
- fix: add the CLI verb over openStore + readLedger + clearMigrationFailure, test it on a temp store

## Expected impact
The operator recovers a refused store with one command instead of SQL against the operator's file. Could break: nothing existing; a new CLI only.

## Evaluation
Claim: resilience - a refused store is recoverable through a named door
Before: 0 doors call clearMigrationFailure (grep over app lib pipeline workers)
After: 1 door, its test clears a seeded mark on a temp store and migrate then runs
Method: probe - the grep is taken; the CLI lives in pipeline/, outside this round's paths
Result: better
Gate: none
evidence:
packages/kernel/src/migrate.ts:27
packages/kernel/src/migrate.ts:210
$ grep -rn clearMigrationFailure app lib pipeline workers -> (no output)
instrument: a pipeline CLI test (node lane) that seeds a mark on a temp GRAVITONE_STORE_PATH, runs the clear verb, and asserts migrate applies afterwards

title: The migration failure mark is written after a step fails, not before it runs
body:
## Summary
migrations:error-propagation asks for a failed-at mark 'set before the step runs, cleared only by its success'; migrate.ts writes it only after a step reports failure, so a process that dies mid-step leaves no mark.

## Description
packages/kernel/src/migrate.ts:197-203 writes the mark in its own tx after the step tx returns an error. A step that kills the process (OOM on a table rebuild, a native crash, a kill during a long boot) rolls back and leaves nothing: every next boot re-runs it, crash-looping with no record of which step. The registry map already records this as the pair's deviation (2026-10-19). Fixed: insert the mark (reason 'in progress') in its own tx before the step and DELETE it inside the step's tx; the existing failure path overwrites it with the real reason. Depends on the operator door card above: once a kill mid-migration strands the store, clearing must be one command.

## Flow
- boot -> migrate -> step k tx -> process killed
- next boot: no mark, step k re-runs, dies again
- fix: mark before, clear in the step's own transaction; crash.ts-driven test kills a child mid-step and asserts the mark stands

## Expected impact
A crash-looping migration names its step on the next boot instead of looping silently. Could break: an interrupted dev boot now needs the clear command (the trade the technique accepts).

## Evaluation
Claim: resilience - a step that kills its process leaves a standing, named mark
Before: 0 marks after a child process is killed inside a step (by construction: the mark is written only on a returned error)
After: 1 mark naming module and version
Method: simulation - walked migrate.ts:185-205 for kill-before-commit; the kill harness (packages/kernel/src/crash.ts) is not wired to migrate yet
Result: unmeasurable
Gate: none
instrument: a crash test that spawns a child running migrate with a step that blocks (e.g. a busy loop in a user function or a held lock), kills it, and reads _migration_failures from the parent

title: The Ledger strip computes all seven facets per day to read one
body:
## Summary
readStrip calls countEvents once per strip day, and each call runs 16 statements (total, head, 7 facets x GROUP BY + sum) while the strip reads only the actorKind facet.

## Description
app/(studio)/ledger/_ledger/read.ts:175-185 loops over the strip's days and calls countEvents(store, {...kernel, since, until}) for each, then reads facet 'actorKind' and total. packages/kernel/src/events-count.ts:74-89 always computes every entry of GROUPS. Fixed: countEvents takes an optional `facets` list (default all) and readStrip asks for ['actorKind'] - 4 statements a day instead of 16. A kernel option plus one caller outside this round's paths.

## Flow
- open /ledger -> readStrip -> N days x countEvents
- each countEvents -> 2 + 7 x 2 statements, each a scan over the day's window
- fix: facets option in events-count.ts; readStrip passes ['actorKind']; time readStrip at 50k events before/after

## Expected impact
The Ledger route's strip does a quarter of the statements per render. Could break: nothing if the default stays 'all facets'.

## Evaluation
Claim: performance - statements per strip render
Before: 16 statements per strip day (counted from events-count.ts:72-78)
After: 4 per day (total, head, actorKind GROUP BY, its sum)
Method: probe - the statement count is read off the code; the timing at 50k rows needs the route's fixture and is outside this round's paths
Result: better
Gate: none
evidence:
app/(studio)/ledger/_ledger/read.ts:182 const c = countEvents(store, { ...kernel, since, until });
packages/kernel/src/events-count.ts:74 const facets: FacetCount[] = GROUPS.map((g) => {
instrument: a next-server timing case: readStrip over a 50k-event temp store, statements counted through a wrapped Reader, before and after the facets option

title: A damaged blob cannot be healed by putting its bytes again
body:
## Summary
blob.put() returns ok without writing when a file of the right SIZE already sits at the address, so a blob read() reports as damaged stays damaged however often the source bytes are put again.

## Description
packages/kernel/src/blob.ts:90 short-circuits on size; :120 read() re-hashes and returns internal 'does not hash to its name; the file is damaged'. Bit rot or a hand edit that keeps the length leaves a file put() will never replace. Fixed: put() keeps the size fast path, but when read() has reported damage (or on an explicit `repair`), it rewrites through tmp + rename; or put() compares a hash of the existing file when sizes match and the file is small. The cost of hashing hundreds of MB on every idempotent put is the reason this is not Lane A.

## Flow
- put(bytes) -> file at address
- a same-length corruption of the file
- read(ref) -> internal damaged
- put(bytes) again -> ok, file unchanged; read still damaged

## Expected impact
A damaged media blob can be restored from its source. Could break: put latency on large files if the check is unconditional.

## Evaluation
Claim: resilience - a damaged blob is repairable
Before: 0 of 1 damaged blobs healed by re-put (walked blob.ts:90)
After: 1 of 1, with put latency on an undamaged 100 MB blob measured on both arms
Method: simulation - walked put/read; the test is S but the design choice (hash on put vs a repair verb) is the arm to measure
Result: unmeasurable
Gate: none
evidence:
packages/kernel/src/blob.ts:90 if ((await sizeOf(file)) === ref.bytes) return ok(ref);
packages/kernel/src/blob.ts:120
instrument: blob.test case: put, overwrite the file with same-length different bytes, put again, read -> ok; plus a put timing on a 100 MB buffer for both arms
drain_note: trade-off for the operator: heal on every same-length re-put vs a repair verb; built then reverted (5f7cef2c)

title: countEvents re-scans for the type and lane groups' sums it already took
body:
## Summary
Each facet runs its own count(*)/count(col) query, and type/typeGroup and lane/laneGroup share the same WHERE, so two of the sixteen statements re-scan a window already counted.

## Description
packages/kernel/src/events-count.ts:78 runs `SELECT count(*), count(col)` per GROUPS entry. For type and typeGroup the left-out facet is the same (`type`), so `n` is identical; count(type_group) can be taken in the same statement as count(type). Merging per distinct WHERE gives 5 sum statements instead of 7.

## Flow
- countEvents -> 7 sum statements
- fix: one sum statement per distinct left-out facet, selecting count(col) for each column under it
- time countEvents at 50k rows before/after

## Expected impact
Fewer scans per count, compounding with the strip card above. Could break: the facet/none arithmetic if a column is paired with the wrong WHERE.

## Evaluation
Claim: performance - statements per countEvents
Before: 16 statements
After: 14 statements
Method: probe - counted from the code; no timing taken
Result: better
Gate: none
evidence:
packages/kernel/src/events-count.ts:32-40 (GROUPS: typeGroup and laneGroup share their facet)
packages/kernel/src/events-count.ts:78
instrument: events.time.test timing at 50k events plus a statement counter on a wrapped Reader; the existing facet assertions are the regression net

title: blob.put and blob.has can reject although they promise a Result and a boolean
body:
## Summary
put()'s catch awaits rm(tmp, {force: true}), which still throws on EPERM/EBUSY (Windows, a held file), and has() lets a non-ENOENT stat error escape, so both promises can reject past their Result/boolean contract.

## Description
packages/kernel/src/blob.ts:102 `await rm(tmp, { force: true })` inside the catch: force only silences ENOENT. :108 has() awaits sizeOf, which rethrows anything but ENOENT (:52). Callers that `await store.put(...)` and branch on `.ok` get an unhandled rejection instead. Fixed: `.catch(() => undefined)` on the cleanup (the put error is the one to report) and has() returning false on a stat error it cannot read.

## Flow
- put on Windows with an indexer holding the tmp -> write fails -> rm(tmp) EPERM -> put rejects
- has() on an unreadable fan-out dir -> rejects

## Expected impact
The blob port keeps its never-throws contract on Windows. Could break: nothing.

## Evaluation
Claim: resilience - promises that resolve to their declared type on every path
Before: 2 paths reject (walked)
After: 0
Method: simulation - an EPERM on rm cannot be produced on demand without an fs seam the module does not have
Result: unmeasurable
Gate: none
instrument: a blob.test case with an injectable fs (or vi.mock of node:fs/promises) whose rm and stat throw EPERM
